title: The Atlas manufactures case law in advance through hypothetical Facilitator Scenarios
content:
A.1.2.2.2.28 defines the Facilitator Scenario Type: a Supporting Document under a single Facilitator Action Tenet containing a "hypothetical fact pattern that illustrates the application of its parent Facilitator Action Tenet," which "should be as concrete in its details as possible, so as to be helpful to the Facilitators' decision-making." Each carries a binary **Finding** — Aligned if the Target Document logic was not breached, Misaligned if it was — plus **Additional Guidance** on "the specific aspects of the Scenario that were salient" and what follow-up or investigation is appropriate.

The non-obvious move is that these are *hypothetical*. Common-law systems get case law only from disputes that actually happen, which means the boundaries of a rule are unknown until someone tests them, usually at cost. The Atlas synthesizes the corpus up front: a rule ships with worked examples on both sides of the line before any controversy exists.

The naming discipline reinforces the case-law framing — the example given is "Crafter approves pull request authored by Prime Team," a specific act by a specific role, not an abstraction. And a Scenario's name may only be numbered if there are duplicates, keeping citations by description rather than by index.

The cost is that Scenarios are authored, so they encode their author's view of where the line falls, without the adversarial pressure a real dispute would supply. The Additional Guidance component is what keeps them honest — it must say *why* the finding came out as it did, exposing the reasoning to challenge rather than just the verdict.
description: Scenarios hang off an Action Tenet as concrete fact patterns with an explicit Aligned/Misaligned Finding plus guidance on how facilitators should respond.
